reason: Rich cross-verified data across seven independent sources fully document Betelgeuse's immense physical scale, 2019 surface ejection, shrinking observations, and 2023 asteroid occultation.
story: In the shoulder of Orion lies Betelgeuse, an aging red supergiant so immense that if placed at the center of our Solar System, its churning surface would swallow Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and stretch beyond the orbit of Jupiter. Yet despite being roughly ten million years old—a mere toddler compared to our middle-aged Sun—Betelgeuse is already in its death throes. In late 2019, skywatchers panicked when the star abruptly lost nearly two-thirds of its visual brightness, plummeting out of the top twenty brightest stars in the night sky. Many feared an imminent supernova. However, observations from observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope revealed a startling reality: Betelgeuse had literally blown off a huge portion of its surface in a titanic Surface Mass Ejection, spewing 400 billion times more mass than a typical solar coronal mass ejection. As this fractured stellar matter drifted away and cooled, it formed a massive dust veil that temporarily blocked its light.
angle: If swapped with our Sun, Betelgeuse's outer edge would engulf the orbit of Jupiter, and in 2019 it literally blew off a massive piece of its visible surface in a never-before-seen stellar convulsion.

claims.claim: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star situated in the constellation Orion.
If placed at the center of our Solar System, Betelgeuse would extend past the orbit of Jupiter.
Betelgeuse is approximately 10 million years old, making it far younger than our Sun.
Astronomers calculate that Betelgeuse will end its life by exploding as a supernova within roughly 100,000 years.
When Betelgeuse detonates as a supernova, the explosion will be bright enough to be visible from Earth during daylight.
Betelgeuse is normally one of the ten brightest stars visible in the night sky.
In late 2019, Betelgeuse dimmed dramatically, causing it to fall completely out of the top twenty brightest stars.
The dramatic 2019 dimming was caused by an ejection of visible surface material that cooled into an obscuring dust cloud.
Betelgeuse was the first extrasolar star to have the angular size of its photosphere directly measured.
Interferometric monitoring on Mount Wilson demonstrated that Betelgeuse's diameter shrank by more than 15 percent between 1993 and the late 2000s.
Measured diameters of Betelgeuse vary by roughly 30 to 35 percent depending on the wavelength of light used.
The surface of Betelgeuse contains immense convective cells that carry gas and heat into its circumstellar environment.
Betelgeuse has historically exhibited a regular brightness pulsation rhythm of roughly 400 to 425 days.
The traditional name Betelgeuse originates from an Arabic term meaning the hand of Orion.
In December 2023, the main-belt asteroid 319 Leona passed directly in front of Betelgeuse, causing a rare occultation.
The narrow path of visibility for the December 2023 Leona occultation stretched across southern Europe, southern Florida, and Mexico.

disputed: Supernova timing: sources range from within 100,000 years to within a million years; scripts should state 'likely within the next 100,000 years, according to astronomers'.
Distance to Betelgeuse: estimates span 400 to over 700 light-years across historical and modern measurements; scripts should attribute distance as 'roughly 500 to 700 light-years away'.

Primary cause of the 2019 dimming: while Hubble studies attribute it to an ejected dust shroud, alternative submillimetre studies suggested giant cool starspots or intersecting natural pulsation minima; scripts should present the cooling dust cloud from a surface mass ejection as the leading Hubble explanation.
Initial stellar mass: estimates vary between roughly 10 and 21 times the mass of the Sun; scripts should state 'between 10 and 20 times the mass of our Sun'.
